mainTopic: Using another person's land without permission: swept-in trees, an ancestral field held by a נכרי, planting a field, and rebuilding a ruin
overview: After closing an earlier point, the גמרא turns to the משנה's case of olive trees that a river carried into someone else's field. Two reports of ריש לקיש's words explain when the fruit is split and when one side takes all of it, using arguments about ערלה and what each owner could have planted instead. A ברייתא adds that the tree owner may not uproot his trees, and רבי יוחנן says the reason is ישוב ארץ ישראל. Next the גמרא studies רבי יהודה's ruling that one who sharecrops 'שדה אבותיו' for a נכרי must tithe before giving the נכרי his share. After a challenge from a ברייתא about a מציק, the גמרא concludes that the phrase means his own family's field, and that the duty to tithe is a penalty meant to push him to buy the field back. Then רב and שמואל argue about paying someone who planted another person's field without permission, and a story shows how רב's view was learned. Finally, רב נחמן and רב ששת argue whether someone who rebuilt another person's ruin may take back his materials. The final ruling, given by רבי יוחנן, continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing words of the previous discussion: not counting the expenses
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of an earlier discussion. The measure being discussed is counted without the expenses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Not including the expense.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of the earlier discussion about the measure of oil in the משנה. They wrap it up before the גמרא moves to the next case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount of oil being measured is counted on its own, without subtracting the costs of processing the olives into oil. With this point settled, the earlier topic is closed.

keyTerms.meaning: Expense, the cost of producing (here, processing the olives into oil)

phrases.english: Not including the expense.
phrases.notes: This finishes an earlier discussion. The oil amount is counted without taking off the cost of processing the olives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The measure is calculated without counting processing expenses.

steps.title: ריש לקיש limits the case: uprooted with their clods, and after three years
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a river sweeping olive trees away. עולא quotes ריש לקיש: the משנה's ruling to split the fruit applies only when the trees were uprooted with their clods of earth, and only after three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'A river swept away his olive trees.' עולא said in the name of ריש לקיש: The משנה taught this only when the trees were uprooted together with their clods of earth, and only after three years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the opening words of the משנה's next case. Then ריש לקיש narrows when the משנה's ruling of splitting the fruit applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה ruled that the tree owner and the field owner split the fruit, since each can say 'my part made it grow.' ריש לקיש adds two conditions. First, the trees came with their own clods of earth, so the tree owner really can claim his soil fed them. Second, the ruling is about fruit that grows after three years.

keyTerms.meaning: A river swept away (flooded and carried off)
They only taught this when, a formula that narrows a teaching
Clods of earth (the soil around the roots)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the משנה's simple rule of splitting the fruit depends on specific facts: the soil came along with the trees, and the time period is past three years.

phrases.english: A river swept away his olive trees.
Ulla said in the name of Reish Lakish:
They taught this only where they were uprooted with their clods of earth,
and after three years.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's split of the fruit applies only to trees uprooted with their clods, and only to fruit after three years.

steps.title: During the first three years, all the fruit goes to the tree owner
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש continues: within the first three years, all the fruit belongs to the tree owner. The tree owner can say, 'Even if you had planted these trees yourself, could you have eaten the fruit in the first three years?'
steps.simpleTranslation: But within the three years, everything belongs to the owner of the olive trees. He can say to the field owner: 'If you had planted these trees within these three years, would you have been allowed to eat the fruit?'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains the other side of his rule: what happens during the first three years. He also gives the tree owner's argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fruit of a newly planted tree is forbidden for three years (ערלה). If the fruit counted as growing from the field owner's land, it would be like a new planting and forbidden. The fruit is only allowed because it counts as growing from the old trees and their own clods, so the tree owner can claim all of it.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the olive trees
Would you have eaten? (meaning: you could not have)

steps.confusionAlert: The tree owner is not saying the field owner's land did nothing. He is saying the field owner cannot claim credit for the fruit, because if the fruit came from his land, it would be forbidden as ערלה.

phrases.english: But within the three years,
everything belongs to the owner of the olive trees.

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי אַתְּ נְטַעְתְּ בְּתוֹךְ שָׁלֹשׁ,
phrases.english: Because he can say to him: If you had planted within the three years,
would you have eaten?
phrases.notes: Fruit of a newly planted tree is forbidden for its first three years (ערלה), so the answer is no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל בְּתוֹךְ שָׁלֹשׁ הַכֹּל שֶׁל בַּעַל הַזֵּיתִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes ריש לקיש's statement by explaining the first three years and giving the reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Within three years all the fruit belongs to the tree owner, since the field owner could not have eaten fruit from new plantings (ערלה).

steps.title: Challenge: the field owner could have planted his own trees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the field owner can't answer back: 'If I had planted my own trees, after three years I would eat all the fruit. Now I only get half with you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the field owner say to him: 'If I had planted my own trees, after three years I would have eaten all the fruit. Now you are eating half of it with me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges ריש לקיש's reasoning. It gives the field owner a strong reply to the tree owner's argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The field owner could have pulled out the swept-in trees and planted his own. Then, after three years, he would get all the fruit. By leaving the tree owner's trees in place, he loses half the fruit later. So he should get something in return during the first three years.

keyTerms.meaning: But let him say to him, introducing a counter-argument

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
If I had planted,
phrases.notes: The field owner means: if I had pulled out your trees and planted my own instead.

phrases.aramaic: לְאַחַר שָׁלֹשׁ הֲוָה אָכֵילְנָא לֵיהּ כּוּלֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: after three years I would have eaten all of it.
Now you are eating half with me!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning given for the tree owner in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's ruling that all the fruit in the first three years goes to the tree owner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The field owner gives up the chance to plant his own trees and own all the fruit after three years. Since he lets the tree owner share later, he should get a share during the first three years.

steps.title: רבין's version: split during three years, all to field owner afterward
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports ריש לקיש's ruling the opposite way: the split applies within the first three years, and after three years all the fruit belongs to the field owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רבין came, he said in the name of ריש לקיש: The משנה's ruling to split applies only when the trees were uprooted with their clods of earth, and only within the first three years. After three years, everything goes to the land owner, because he can say: 'If I had planted my own trees, after three years wouldn't I eat all of it?'
steps.whatsHappening: Because the first version ran into a problem in step 4, the גמרא now brings a different report of ריש לקיש's words, from רבין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version flips the timing. The split is during the first three years, and after three years the field owner takes everything. His argument is that once three years pass, his own trees would have given him all the fruit, so the stranger's trees should not cut his share in half.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing a teaching)
With their clods of earth (the roots still in their original soil)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In the first version (steps 2-3), the tree owner gets everything in the first three years. In רבין's version, the fruit is split in the first three years and the field owner gets everything afterward.

phrases.english: Rather, when Ravin came,
he said in the name of Reish Lakish:
They taught this only where they were uprooted with their clods of earth
and within the first three years,
but after three years
everything belongs to the owner of the land.
Because he can say to him:
If I had planted my own trees,

phrases.aramaic: לְאַחַר שָׁלֹשׁ, מִי לָא הֲוָה אָכֵילְנָא לֵיהּ כּוּלֵּיהּ?
phrases.english: after three years, wouldn't I have eaten all of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין, אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4 by replacing the first version of ריש לקיש's words with רבין's version.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate transmission of the same אמורא's statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ריש לקיש gave all the early fruit to the tree owner, which left the field owner's complaint unanswered.
steps.terutzMaskana: ריש לקיש actually said the fruit is split during the first three years and goes entirely to the field owner afterward.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Within three years the fruit is split; after three years all of it goes to the land owner.

steps.title: Why can't the tree owner object to splitting in the first three years?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: let the tree owner say, 'Even with your own trees you'd eat nothing in the first three years, so why do you get half now?'
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say to him: 'If you had planted, you wouldn't have eaten anything in the first three years. Now you're eating half together with me?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבין's version. It asks why the field owner should get half of the fruit during the first three years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fruit from the first three years of a tree is ערלה, so a field owner with his own new trees would have eaten nothing from them. The tree owner argues that the field owner loses nothing from those years and so should not get half.

keyTerms.meaning: But let him say to him (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: But let him say to him:
phrases.notes: "He" here is the tree owner, speaking to the field owner.

phrases.english: If you had planted,
within three years you would not have eaten,
and now you eat half together with me?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first half of רבין's version, the split during the first three years.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבין's ruling that the fruit is split during the first three years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The field owner would get nothing from his own trees during the first three years, so he has no loss that would entitle him to half.

steps.title: Young trees would have let him grow vegetables underneath
steps.stepSummary: The field owner can answer that his own young trees would be thin, and he could have grown chard and vegetables under them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he can say to him: 'If I had planted, they would be thin, and I would plant chard and vegetables underneath them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of step 6. The field owner really does lose something during the first three years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Your grown trees cast heavy shade, while my young trees would have been thin. Under thin saplings I could have grown vegetables and made money. Since your trees took away that profit, I deserve half of the fruit even in the first three years.
steps.whatToRemember: In רבין's version, the field owner gets half during the first three years because of the vegetables he could have grown under young trees, and all the fruit afterward because his own grown trees would have been fully his.

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
If I had planted,
they would be thin,
and I would sow chard and vegetables underneath them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a hidden loss to the field owner
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The field owner loses nothing during the first three years, since his own fruit would be forbidden then too.
steps.terutzMaskana: He loses the vegetables he could have grown under his own thin saplings, so he deserves half.

steps.title: The tree owner cannot uproot his trees
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if the tree owner wants to take his olive trees back, we do not listen to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: If the other one said, 'I am taking my olive trees,' we don't listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new detail about the same case of the swept trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the question was how to divide the fruit. Here the tree owner wants to end the arrangement by uprooting his trees and moving them, and the ברייתא does not allow it.

keyTerms.meaning: The other one (here, the tree owner)
We do not listen to him

phrases.english: It was taught: If the other one said, "I am taking my olive trees" –
we do not listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new ruling about the same משנה case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tree owner may not uproot and take back his trees.

steps.title: What is the reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the tree owner isn't allowed to take his own trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ברייתא's ruling. This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trees belong to him, so it seems strange to stop him from taking them. The גמרא wants to know what reason could override his ownership.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the ruling of step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the owner may not take back his own trees.

steps.title: Because of settling ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the reason is ישוב ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Because of settling ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question of step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Uprooting healthy, rooted trees harms the land. To keep ארץ ישראל built up and planted, the חכמים did not let the owner pull them out.

keyTerms.meaning: Keeping ארץ ישראל settled and built up

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that ישוב ארץ ישראל can be strong enough to limit what a person may do with his own property.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Because of the settling of the Land of Israel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: מִשּׁוּם יִשּׁוּב אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling protects ישוב ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה praises the explanation
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה says that a reason like this one takes a great scholar to explain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: Something like this needs a great person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה comments on רבי יוחנן's answer and closes this short discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ירמיה is saying the reason is not obvious. Only a great חכם like רבי יוחנן could see that the rule comes from ישוב ארץ ישראל and not from ordinary property law.
steps.whatToRemember: The tree owner may not uproot his trees because of ישוב ארץ ישראל, a reason רבי ירמיה called worthy of a great scholar.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
Something like this needs a great one.
phrases.notes: He means it takes a great חכם to come up with a reason like this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: כְּגוֹן דָּא צְרִיכָא רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Praises the answer given in step 10.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The reason of ישוב ארץ ישראל is accepted and praised as a deep insight.

steps.title: A man working his ancestors' field for a non-Jew
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה in דמאי: רבי יהודה says that one who works his ancestors' field for a נכרי must tithe first and then give the נכרי his share.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned there: רבי יהודה says: One who takes on his ancestors' field from a נכרי tithes, and then gives him his share.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a משנה from another מסכתא. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה rules that this worker must take off מעשר from the produce first, and only then hand the נכרי his share from tithed produce. The גמרא now has to work out what 'his ancestors' field' means and why the נכרי's share needs tithing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: One who takes on a field to work it for a share of the crop

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in דמאי 6:2.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
One who takes on his ancestors' field from a gentile to work it –
tithes, and then gives him his share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the swept olive trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, one who works his ancestors' field for a נכרי tithes everything before giving the נכרי his share.

steps.title: First assumption: 'שדה אבותיו' means any field in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא first assumed that 'שדה אבותיו' refers to any field in ארץ ישראל, which is called his ancestors' field because it belonged to אברהם, יצחק and יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They first assumed: what is 'his ancestors' field'? It is any field in ארץ ישראל. Why call it 'his ancestors' field'? Because the whole land is the field of אברהם, יצחק and יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts working out the משנה from step 12 by giving a first reading of the words 'שדה אבותיו'. This reading sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this reading, the Jew has no personal claim to the field. The נכרי owns it fairly, and it is 'ancestral' only because all of ארץ ישראל was promised to the אבות. That makes the tithe question harder, because the produce seems to grow on a נכרי's land.

keyTerms.meaning: They assumed (a first idea, which may later be rejected)

steps.confusionAlert: 'סברוה' means this is only a first assumption. Do not treat it as the final explanation. The very next challenge (step 16) puts pressure on it.

phrases.english: They assumed:
What is meant by 'his ancestors' field'?
The Land of Israel.
And why do they call it 'his ancestors' field'?
Because it is the field of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a first reading of the key phrase in the משנה quoted in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'שדה אבותיו' is taken to mean any field in ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: A non-Jew's ownership does not cancel tithes
steps.stepSummary: On this reading, the תנא holds that a נכרי who owns land in ארץ ישראל does not remove its produce from the obligation of מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא holds that a נכרי's ownership in ארץ ישראל does not free the land from the obligation to tithe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first reason why the Jewish worker must tithe, even though a נכרי owns the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a נכרי's purchase removed the land's holiness, there would be no tithe obligation at all. By saying 'אין קנין לנכרי', the תנא keeps the land's duty to give מעשר in place. This explains why tithing applies at all. The next step explains why the worker must tithe the owner's share too.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-Jew's ownership does not take effect (here, for removing holiness)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known מחלוקת about whether a non-Jew's ownership removes the holiness of land in ארץ ישראל. Here it is used as one building block of רבי יהודה's ruling.

phrases.english: And he holds:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the תנא of the משנה, רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: A non-Jew's ownership in the Land of Israel does not have the power
to remove it from the obligation of tithes.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקָסָבַר אֵין קִנְיָן לְנׇכְרִי בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first legal reason behind the ruling, following the reading in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נכרי's ownership does not cancel the מעשר obligation on land in ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: A sharecropper is like a tenant farmer paying a debt
steps.stepSummary: The תנא also holds that a מקבל (sharecropper) is like a חוכר (tenant farmer). His payment to the owner counts as paying a debt, so he must tithe first and then give the owner his share.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sharecropper is like a tenant farmer. A tenant farmer must tithe and pay the owner whether or not the field produced, because he is paying off a debt. So too, a sharecropper is like someone paying a debt, so he tithes and then gives the owner his share.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second reason. It explains why the worker must tithe even the part of the crop that goes to the נכרי owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חוכר owes a fixed amount no matter what grows, so the produce is his own and he is simply paying a debt with it. The תנא treats the מקבל the same way. The owner's share counts as the worker's own produce used to pay a debt, so it must be tithed before he hands it over.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharecropper who pays the owner a percentage of the crop
A tenant farmer who pays the owner a fixed amount of produce

steps.confusionAlert: Usually a מקבל and a חוכר are different: one pays a percentage, the other a fixed amount. Here the תנא says they are alike only in one way: both are treated as paying a debt.

phrases.english: And a sharecropper is like a tenant farmer.
Just as a tenant farmer,
whether the field produced or did not produce,
must tithe and give to him,
because he is like one paying his debt.
So too, a sharecropper also
is like one paying his debt,
so he tithes and then gives to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the second reason, which completes the explanation of the משנה under the first reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מקבל is treated like a חוכר paying a debt, so he must tithe before he gives the owner his share.
steps.whatToRemember: Under the first reading, the ruling rests on two ideas: (1) a נכרי's ownership does not cancel מעשר, and (2) a מקבל is like a חוכר paying a debt.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא mention a violent seizer?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא challenges the first reading from a ברייתא in which רבי יהודה speaks of a field received from a מציק נכרי. If any field in ארץ ישראל counts, why does the ברייתא mention a מציק?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said to רב פפי (some say to רב זביד): What about the ברייתא in which רבי יהודה says that one who receives his ancestors' field from a non-Jewish oppressor tithes and then gives him his share? Why mention an oppressor? The same rule should apply even if he is not an oppressor!
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא attacks the first reading using a ברייתא that adds the word 'מציק' to רבי יהודה's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'his ancestors' field' means any field in ארץ ישראל, the ruling should apply to any נכרי owner. Yet the ברייתא speaks only of a מציק, someone who took the field by force. That suggests 'his ancestors' field' means the Jew's own family field that was stolen from him, which weakens the first reading.

keyTerms.meaning: An oppressor who seized land by force
Why specifically this case? (a challenge to a detail that seems unneeded)

steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge pushes the גמרא to rethink what 'שדה אבותיו' means, and it sets up the next approach.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא לְרַב פַּפִּי,
phrases.english: Rav Kahana said to Rav Pappi,
and some say it was to Rav Zevid:
But what about that which is taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Yehuda says:
One who receives his ancestors' field from a non-Jewish oppressor
tithes and then gives to him.
Why specifically an oppressor?
Even if he is not an oppressor, the same should apply!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first reading from steps 13 to 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first assumption (step 13) that 'שדה אבותיו' means any field in ארץ ישראל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא limits the ruling to a field taken by a מציק. If any field counted, that detail would serve no purpose, so 'his ancestors' field' must mean something narrower.

steps.title: A new reading: the נכרי's ownership counts, and a sharecropper is not like a tenant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reverses both assumptions of the first reading. A נכרי's ownership does remove land in ארץ ישראל from מעשר, and a מקבל is not like a חוכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: in truth, a נכרי's ownership of land in ארץ ישראל does take its produce out of the obligation of מעשר. And a sharecropper is not like a tenant farmer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב כהנא's challenge by throwing out the first explanation and starting fresh with the opposite two assumptions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 14 the תנא held that a נכרי's ownership does not remove מעשר. Now he holds that it does. In step 15 a מקבל was like a חוכר and was paying a debt. Now a מקבל is not like a חוכר: the owner's share is simply the owner's own produce. So by basic law there should be no duty to tithe before handing it over. The duty רבי יהודה states must be something extra, and the next steps explain what.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; signals that the earlier explanation is dropped
A non-Jew's legal ownership of land
To remove the produce from the obligation of tithing
Is not like a tenant farmer

steps.confusionAlert: This is the exact opposite of steps 14–15 on both points. Don't mix the two readings together.

phrases.english: Rather: in truth, a non-Jew has ownership
in the Land of Israel to remove the produce from tithing,
and a sharecropper is not like a tenant farmer.
phrases.notes: So when he hands over the owner's share, he isn't paying a debt. He's giving the owner what is already the owner's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב כהנא's challenge by replacing the first reading
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reverses the underlying assumptions about the law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A נכרי's ownership does not remove מעשר, and a מקבל is like a חוכר who pays a debt
steps.terutzMaskana: A נכרי's ownership does remove מעשר, and a מקבל is not like a חוכר

steps.title: His ancestors' field means his actual family's field
steps.stepSummary: On the new reading, 'שדה אבותיו' is no longer any field in ארץ ישראל. It is a field that really belonged to his own ancestors.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what does 'his ancestors' field' mean? It literally means his own ancestors' field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא redefines the phrase 'שדה אבותיו' to fit the new reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 the phrase meant any field in ארץ ישראל, since it belonged to אברהם, יצחק and יעקב. Now it means a field his own family owned, which a נכרי took. This fits the ברייתא's mention of a מציק נכרי, which is what bothered רב כהנא.

keyTerms.meaning: A field that literally belonged to his own family

phrases.english: And what is 'his ancestors' field'?
It is literally his ancestors' field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the new reading by redefining the key phrase
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'שדה אבותיו' means any field in ארץ ישראל
steps.terutzMaskana: 'שדה אבותיו' means his own family's field, taken by a נכרי

steps.title: The penalty falls only on the heir, because he loves the field
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן fined only the person whose family owned the field, because he would eagerly sharecrop it. Nobody else was fined.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only him that the רבנן penalized, because the field is extra dear to him and he will go and take it as a sharecropper. But an ordinary person was not penalized.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that tithing first is a penalty, and says who receives it and why only that person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since by basic law there is no duty to tithe, the requirement is a קנס from the רבנן. They aimed it only at the heir, because his love for his family's land makes him likely to sharecrop it for the נכרי. An ordinary person has no such pull, so there was no need to fine him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that רבי יהודה's ruling is a rabbinic penalty, not basic tithing law. That explains why it is so limited.

phrases.english: And it is him that the Sages penalized,
phrases.notes: The penalty is making him tithe before giving the owner his share.

phrases.english: because since it is extra dear to him
he will go and take it as a sharecropper.
But an ordinary person, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the heir must tithe, given that basic law does not require it
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tithing first is a rabbinic penalty that applies only to the heir of the field, not to anyone else

steps.title: Why penalize him at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the purpose of the penalty is.
steps.simpleTranslation: And as for him, what is the reason the רבנן penalized him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knows who was penalized. Now it asks why the רבנן wanted to penalize him at all, and sets up רבי יוחנן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 explained why the penalty is limited to the heir. It did not explain what the penalty is meant to achieve. Working a field for its owner is not obviously wrong, so the גמרא wants the goal behind the fine.

phrases.english: And for him, what is the reason
that the Sages penalized him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the purpose behind the penalty described in step 19
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The goal the רבנן had in penalizing the heir

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: so the field will be clearly his
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the penalty is meant to make the field fully his. It pushes him to buy it outright instead of sharecropping it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: so that it will be clearly in his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question: the penalty is there to get the family field back into Jewish hands for good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because sharecropping now costs him extra, it becomes a bad deal. He is better off buying the field from the נכרי outright. Then the land is fully his again.

keyTerms.meaning: So that it will be clearly and fully his

steps.whatToRemember: The rule makes sharecropping unattractive, so the heir buys back his family's land instead.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
so that it will be clearly in his hands.
phrases.notes: Literally 'clear in his hand.' The extra cost of sharecropping should push him to buy the field outright.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא בָּרָה בְּיָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The penalty pushes the heir to buy the field outright, so it will be fully his

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: a ruling like this needs a great sage
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה remarks that a ruling like this one needs a great sage to explain it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: something like this needs a great sage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה comments on רבי יוחנן's explanation. He says that only a great sage could uncover the reason behind such a ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for the penalty is hidden. Nothing in the text of the ruling hints at encouraging a purchase. רבי ירמיה's remark highlights how deep רבי יוחנן's explanation is.

keyTerms.meaning: Needs a great person (to explain it)

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: tithing first is a penalty on the heir alone, meant to push him to buy back his family's land.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
Something like this needs a great sage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה: כְּגוֹן דָּא צְרִיכָא רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Comments on רבי יוחנן's answer
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ruling like this requires a great sage to explain its reason

steps.title: Planting in someone else's field without permission
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל disagree about how much the field owner must pay a person who planted his field without permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if someone goes into his friend's field and plants it without permission, רב says the court appraises it for him, and he gets the lower amount. שמואל says the court estimates how much a person would be willing to pay to have this field planted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument between רב and שמואל about a person who planted trees in someone else's field without asking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner gained something, so he has to pay. In רב's view, the court looks at two numbers, what the planter spent and how much the field went up in value, and the planter gets only the lower one. In שמואל's view, the owner pays the normal price people pay to have a field like this planted.

keyTerms.meaning: He is at a disadvantage: he gets the lower of the two amounts

phrases.english: It was stated: one who goes down into his friend's field
and planted it without permission,
רב said: we appraise for him,
and his hand is on the lower side.
phrases.notes: In other words, the planter gets whichever of the two amounts is smaller.

phrases.english: And שמואל said: we estimate
how much a person would want to give
for this field, to have it planted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הַיּוֹרֵד לְתוֹךְ שְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ וּנְטָעָהּ שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of שדה אבותיו.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: appraise, and the planter gets the lower amount. שמואל: the owner pays the usual price for having such a field planted.

steps.title: רב פפא: they talk about two different kinds of fields
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says רב and שמואל do not argue. One is talking about a field meant for planting, and the other about a field that is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: they do not disagree. Here it is a field that is usually planted, and there it is a field that is not usually planted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא makes peace between רב and שמואל by saying each one is talking about a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the field is the kind people plant anyway, the owner really benefited, so he pays the normal planting price (שמואל). If the field is not meant for planting, the owner did not ask for this, so the planter only gets the lower amount (רב).

keyTerms.meaning: Meant to be planted (normally used for trees)

steps.confusionAlert: The first כאן goes with שמואל, not רב. A field meant for planting gets שמואל's full planting price.

phrases.english: רב פפא said: and they do not disagree:
here, in a field that is meant to be planted,
there, in a field that is not meant to be planted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the argument from step 23 by splitting the cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each opinion applies to a different kind of field.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and שמואל seem to argue about the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל is talking about a field meant for planting. רב is talking about a field not meant for planting.

steps.title: רב's ruling was learned from a case, not said directly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רב never said his ruling outright. It was learned from how he judged a real case.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this ruling of רב was not said directly. It was learned from a story.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a side note about where רב's ruling comes from, and it is setting up a story that it tells next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far רב's opinion looked like a ruling he said word for word. The גמרא says no: we only learn it by looking at how he handled one case. The story comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference, learned from what happened

phrases.english: And this ruling of רב was not stated directly,
rather, it was stated by inference.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא דְּרַב לָאו בְּפֵירוּשׁ אִיתְּמַר, אֶלָּא מִכְּלָלָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains where רב's opinion from step 23 comes from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's ruling is learned from his actions in a case, not from words he said.

steps.title: The field owner says 'I don't want it'
steps.stepSummary: A field owner comes to רב. רב tells him to have it appraised, with the planter getting the lower amount. The owner keeps saying he does not want the trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone came before רב. רב told him: go have it appraised for him. He said: I don't want this. רב said: go have it appraised, and the planter gets the lower amount. He said: I don't want this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins the story that shows where רב's ruling comes from. The owner keeps refusing to pay for trees he never asked for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב first tells the owner to pay, then softens it so the planter only gets the lower amount. When the owner still says he does not want the trees, רב does not push any further. This tells us that if the owner truly does not want the planting, he does not have to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: Go have it appraised for him

phrases.english: For a certain man came before רב,
phrases.notes: This is the owner of the field that was planted.

phrases.english: he said to him: go appraise for him.
He said to him: I don't want it.
He said to him: go appraise for him,
and his hand is on the lower side.
He said to him: I don't want it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells the story that step 25 promised.
steps.raayaObject: Where רב's ruling about the planter comes from.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A real case judged by רב, where the owner refused to pay for trees he did not want.

steps.title: The owner guards the trees, so the planter gets the higher amount
steps.stepSummary: Later רב sees the owner fencing and guarding the trees. He rules that the owner clearly wants them, so the planter gets the higher amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, רב saw that he fenced the field and was guarding it. He told him: you have shown that you are happy with it. Go have it appraised, and the planter gets the higher amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The owner's actions show he really wants the trees, so רב rules strongly in the planter's favor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner kept saying 'I don't want it,' but fencing and guarding the trees showed what he really thought. Once it is clear he is happy with the planting, the planter is no longer at a disadvantage: he gets the higher of the two amounts.

keyTerms.meaning: You have shown what you really think
He has the advantage: he gets the higher of the two amounts

steps.whatToRemember: What a person does can show what he really wants. An owner who refuses the planting may not have to pay. An owner who guards the trees has shown he is happy with them, so the planter gets the higher amount.

phrases.english: In the end, he saw him that he fenced it
and was guarding it.
He said to him: you have revealed your mind
that it is pleasing to you,
go appraise for him,
and his hand is on the upper side.
phrases.notes: Now the planter gets whichever amount is bigger, the opposite of before.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְסוֹף חַזְיֵיהּ דְּגַדְרַהּ וְקָא מְנַטַּר לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in step 26 and gives רב's final ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: If the owner shows by his actions that he wants the planting, the planter gets the higher amount (ידו על העליונה).

steps.title: Can the builder take back his wood and stones?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן and רב ששת disagree about whether someone who rebuilt another person's ruin without permission may take his materials back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: Someone went into his friend's ruined building and rebuilt it without permission. Then he said, 'I am taking my wood and my stones back.' רב נחמן says we listen to him. רב ששת says we do not listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument between two אמוראים. The question is whether a builder who rebuilt without permission may take apart what he built and take back his materials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case is like the planting case in the earlier steps, but here the builder wants his materials back instead of payment. רב נחמן allows it. רב ששת does not, so the building stays and the builder cannot take it apart.

keyTerms.meaning: We listen to him, meaning the court lets him do it
We do not listen to him, meaning the court does not let him

phrases.english: It was stated:
One who goes down into his friend's ruin
and built it up without his permission,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לוֹ: עֵצַיי וַאֲבָנַיי אֲנִי נוֹטֵל,
phrases.english: and he said to him: I am taking my wood and my stones,
רב נחמן says: We listen to him,

phrases.aramaic: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת אָמַר: אֵין שׁוֹמְעִין לוֹ.
phrases.english: רב ששת says: We do not listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case that is like the earlier planting case, this time about building.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן: the builder may take back his wood and stones. רב ששת: he may not.

steps.title: Does רב נחמן follow בית שמאי?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records בית שמאי as allowing it and בית הלל as forbidding it, so רב נחמן seems to follow בית שמאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that בית שמאי say we listen to him, and בית הלל say we do not listen to him. Shall we say that רב נחמן ruled like בית שמאי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן from a ברייתא. In that ברייתא, only בית שמאי agree with his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The halacha almost always follows בית הלל. If רב נחמן's view matches only בית שמאי, his ruling looks hard to accept. So this question is really an attack on רב נחמן.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of הלל, whose rulings are usually the halacha

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says:
בית שמאי say: We listen to him,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אֵין שׁוֹמְעִין לוֹ.
phrases.english: and בית הלל say: We do not listen to him.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא רַב נַחְמָן דְּאָמַר כְּבֵית שַׁמַּאי?
phrases.english: Shall we say that רב נחמן ruled like בית שמאי?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב נחמן's view from step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that we listen to the builder
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא puts רב נחמן's view only with בית שמאי, and the halacha usually follows בית הלל.

steps.title: רב נחמן follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, who teaches the ruling 'we listen to him' with no argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: He ruled like this other תנא, as it was taught: We listen to him. These are the words of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that בית שמאי say we listen to him, and בית הלל say we do not listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there are two versions of this teaching. רב נחמן follows the version of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר gives the ruling 'we listen to him' without any argument, so it seems both בית שמאי and בית הלל agree. Only רבן שמעון בן גמליאל reports an argument between them. So רב נחמן is not going against בית הלל. He follows a different report of what they held.
steps.confusionAlert: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's words here are the same ones quoted in the challenge. The גמרא repeats them to show that they are only one side of a תנאי argument.

phrases.english: He ruled like this תנא,
as it was taught: We listen to him,
these are the words of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says:
בית שמאי say: We listen to him,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים: אֵין שׁוֹמְעִין לוֹ.
phrases.english: and בית הלל say: We do not listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that there are two תנאים who report the views differently
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought בית הלל definitely disagree, so רב נחמן would be following בית שמאי.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, everyone agrees that we listen to the builder, and רב נחמן follows him.

steps.title: What is the final halacha?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the final ruling is, and begins to quote רבי יעקב in the name of רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the conclusion on this? רבי יעקב said in the name of רבי יוחנן:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how we finally rule in this argument. It is setting up the answer, which begins here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides now have support from a תנא, so the גמרא needs a final ruling. It brings רבי יוחנן, through רבי יעקב, to decide.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the conclusion on this matter?

phrases.english: What is the conclusion about it?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: רבי יעקב said that רבי יוחנן said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both views are shown to have support, the גמרא asks for the final halacha.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose view is the halacha, רב נחמן's or רב ששת's?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer, in the name of רבי יוחנן, continues on the next amud.
